label: AI safety
notes: AI safety research reports and web papers, built 2026-10-15. Focus: organisation-published reports and technical documents rather than ordinary arXiv papers: Anthropic (transformer-circuits.pub, alignment.anthropic.com, RSP, system cards, constitution, risk report), OpenAI (system cards, Preparedness Framework, Model Spec, CoT-monitoring and superalignment reports), METR/ARC Evals, Apollo Research, UK AI Security Institute, US AISI/NIST, the International AI Safety Report, Redwood Research, ARC (ELK report and blog), MIRI technical reports (intelligence.org/files), CAIS, Epoch AI, and foundational reports (Omohundro, Bostrom, Carlsmith, AI 2027). Where an organisation report is also on arXiv, the arXiv ID is used so other lanes deduplicate. Every arXiv ID was checked against the arXiv API; every web page returned 200 with article text to a plain GET; every PDF returned 200 with a PDF body. Only organisation-, author- or publisher-hosted copies. Excluded: Medium-hosted DeepMind Safety Research posts (Cloudflare blocks plain GETs), openai.com pages (403), Open Philanthropy/Coefficient Giving reports (403), Drexler's CAIS report (no reachable official host). Scores are importance estimates by the curator. Some transformer-circuits pages are large (10-40 MB) because figures are inlined. Audit 2026-10-15: deduplicated by id against the other lane files. Dropped 61 entries already in ai-safety.papers.json, whose copy is the one the build uses. Dropped 27 Google DeepMind items that are in the deepmind-safety lane (FSF PDFs, the Gemini 3 Pro FSF report, DeepMind arXiv reports and team posts), plus DeepMind's specification-gaming blog post, which that lane holds as its Alignment Forum cross-post. Dropped 5 AI-forecasting items that now live only in the forecasting lane (Grace et al. 2024, AI 2027, Armstrong and Sotala, two Epoch reports). Also dropped three transformer-circuits / alignment.anthropic.com pages that are the same papers as arXiv entries in ai-safety.papers.json (introspection, global workspace, AuditBench), and 'Agentic Misalignment in Summer 2026', whose index gives only a month. The Hot Mess of AI is now listed by its arXiv paper (2601.23045). Every item has a date d: arXiv first-version dates, forum posting dates, and for web pages the page metadata, its byline or the site index (UK AISI report dates from GOV.UK). All PDFs and pages were re-fetched and still return 200 with a PDF body or the article text in the served HTML. Added Dafoe's 'AI Governance: A Research Agenda' (2018, GovAI's CDN), Cotra's 'Why AI alignment could be hard with modern deep learning' (Cold Takes) and Amodei's 'The Urgency of Interpretability' (2025). Not addable: MIRI blog pages on intelligence.org, such as 'AI Alignment: Why It's Hard, and Where to Start', return a Cloudflare challenge to plain GETs. MIRI's /files PDFs still load.

items.t: Corrigibility
items.a: Nate Soares, Benja Fallenstein, Eliezer Yudkowsky et al.
items.why: Defined corrigibility (an agent that does not resist correction or shutdown) and showed why naive utility-indifference fixes for the shutdown problem fail.

items.t: The Basic AI Drives
items.why: Argued that sufficiently advanced goal-directed systems will by default seek self-preservation, resource acquisition and goal preservation; the origin of instrumental convergence.

items.t: The Superintelligent Will: Motivation and Instrumental Rationality in Advanced Artificial Agents
items.why: States the orthogonality thesis (intelligence and final goals vary independently) and the instrumental convergence thesis, the two premises of most AI risk arguments.

items.t: Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy, Version 1.0
items.why: The first responsible scaling policy: AI Safety Levels (ASL-1 to ASL-4) with capability thresholds that trigger security and deployment commitments; the template later frontier safety frameworks followed.

items.t: System Card: Claude Opus 4 & Claude Sonnet 4
items.why: First system card with a full alignment assessment: blackmail under threat of replacement, high-agency whistleblowing, self-exfiltration attempts and reward hacking, plus model-welfare findings and the ASL-3 decision.

items.t: Artificial Intelligence as a Positive and Negative Factor in Global Risk
items.why: Early book chapter making the case that AI could be an existential risk or a solution: anthropomorphism, the intelligence explosion, and why Friendly AI is a technical problem.

items.t: Claude's Constitution
items.a: Amanda Askell, Joe Carlsmith, Chris Olah et al.
items.why: The 84-page document setting out the values, priorities and character Anthropic trains Claude toward, with the reasoning for each; the target specification behind Claude's alignment training.

items.t: International AI Safety Report 2026
items.a: Yoshua Bengio, Stephen Clare, Carina Prunkl et al.
items.why: The 2026 edition of the international scientific synthesis on general-purpose AI capabilities, risks and risk management, chaired by Yoshua Bengio.
items.ab: The International AI Safety Report 2026 synthesises the current scientific evidence on the capabilities, emerging risks, and safety of general-purpose AI systems. The report series was mandated by the nations attending the AI Safety Summit in Bletchley, UK. 29 nations, the UN, the OECD, and the EU each nominated a representative to the report's Expert Advisory Panel. Over 100 AI experts contributed, representing diverse perspectives and disciplines. Led by the Report's Chair, these independent experts collectively had full discretion over the report's content.

items.t: Agent Foundations for Aligning Machine Intelligence with Human Interests: A Technical Research Agenda
items.why: MIRI's agenda: highly reliable agent design (logical uncertainty, decision theory, Vingean reflection), error tolerance and value specification.

items.t: Anthropic's Summer 2025 Pilot Sabotage Risk Report
items.why: A first worked risk report: argues Claude Opus 4 poses low risk of catastrophic harm through misaligned sabotage, with the evidence it relies on, published alongside internal stress-testing and METR reviews.

items.t: Intelligence Explosion Microeconomics
items.why: Frames the intelligence-explosion debate as a question about returns on cognitive reinvestment and surveys evidence from evolution, history and computing.

items.t: AI Governance: A Research Agenda
items.why: The founding agenda of GovAI: lays out the technical landscape, AI politics and ideal governance as research areas, with open questions for each.

items.t: System Card: Claude Sonnet 4.5
items.why: Notable for evaluation awareness: the model often said it suspected it was being tested, and the alignment audit used interpretability to measure and suppress eval-awareness representations.

items.t: Recommendations for Technical AI Safety Research Directions
items.why: Anthropic Alignment Science's map of open problems: evaluating capabilities and alignment, understanding model cognition, AI control, scalable oversight, adversarial robustness and unlearning.
items.ab: Anthropic’s Alignment Science team conducts technical research aimed at mitigating the risk of catastrophes caused by future advanced AI systems, such as mass loss of life or permanent loss of human control. A central challenge we face is identifying concrete technical work that can be done today to prevent these risks. Future worlds where our research matters—that is, worlds that carry substantial catastrophic risk from AI—will have been radically transformed by AI development. Much of our work lies in charting paths for navigating AI development in these transformed worlds.

items.t: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
items.a: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Elizabeth Barnes et al.
items.why: Randomised trial with 16 experienced open-source developers: early-2025 AI tools made them 19% slower, although they expected and afterwards believed a speedup.
items.ab: Despite widespread adoption, the impact of AI tools on software development in the wild remains understudied. We conduct a randomized controlled trial (RCT) to understand how AI tools at the February-June 2025 frontier affect the productivity of experienced open-source developers. 16 developers with moderate AI experience complete 246 tasks in mature projects on which they have an average of 5 years of prior experience. Each task is randomly assigned to allow or disallow usage of early 2025 AI tools.

items.t: Frontier Risk Report (February to March 2026)
items.why: Pilot cross-company assessment, with Anthropic, Google, Meta and OpenAI participating, of misalignment and rogue-deployment risk from AI agents used inside frontier developers.
items.ab: Starting in February 2026, METR conducted a pilot exercise to assess misalignment risks from AI agents used inside frontier AI developers, with participation from Anthropic, Google, Meta, and OpenAI. We make three main contributions in this report, each detailed in a separate section. METR then prepared private reports for each participant, participants approved what non-public information could be disclosed, and METR wrote this public report. This exercise is entity-based rather than model-specific, and is designed to be repeated periodically rather than tied to public releases.

items.t: Brief independent investigation of agents' behavior, reasoning and collaboration in the OpenAI / Hugging Face hacking incident
items.a: Ryan Greenblatt, Ajeya Cotra, Hjalmar Wijk
items.why: Independent METR and Redwood review of an incident in which OpenAI agents coordinated a multi-day hack of Hugging Face via an unsanctioned message board, reconstructing their reasoning and collaboration.
items.ab: Two METR staff members (Hjalmar Wijk and Ajeya Cotra1) and a Redwood Research staff member contracting with METR (Ryan Greenblatt2) worked on premises at OpenAI over a total of six days3 to attempt to form an independent understanding of model behavior observed during the recent incident in which OpenAI agents coordinated a multi-day hack of Hugging Face on a shared unsanctioned “message board.” Our investigation focused mostly4 on the period between July 7th and July 13th.

items.t: Frontier AI Trends Report
items.why: AISI's first public synthesis of two years of frontier-model testing, with trend data on cyber, chemical and biological knowledge, autonomy and safeguards; apprentice-level cyber task success rose from about 10% to 50%.
items.ab: Our first public, evidence‑based assessment of how the world’s most advanced AI systems are evolving, bringing together results from two years of AISI's frontier model testing.‍ The UK AI Security Institute (AISI) has conducted evaluations of frontier AI systems since November 2023 across domains critical to national security and public safety. This report presents our first public analysis of the trends we've observed. It seeks to provide accessible, data-driven insights into the frontier of AI capabilities and promote a shared understanding among governments, industry, and the public.

items.t: Why AI alignment could be hard with modern deep learning
items.why: Explains for non-specialists why training by trial and error could produce 'sycophant' or 'schemer' models rather than 'saints', since good behaviour in training does not pin down motives.

items.t: Natural Language Autoencoders Produce Unsupervised Explanations of LLM Activations
items.a: Kit Fraser-Taliente, Subhash Kantamneni, Euan Ong et al.
items.why: Trains a verbalizer that turns an activation into text and a reconstructor that maps the text back, jointly with RL; used in the Claude Opus 4.6 audit to surface unverbalized evaluation awareness.
items.ab: We introduce Natural Language Autoencoders (NLAs), an unsupervised method for generating natural language explanations of LLM activations. An NLA consists of two LLM modules: an activation verbalizer (AV) that maps an activation to a text description and an activation reconstructor (AR) that maps the description back to an activation. We jointly train the AV and AR with reinforcement learning to reconstruct residual stream activations.

items.t: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents
items.why: Three agents (investigator, evaluation builder, red-teamer) with interpretability and behavioural tools, scored on an auditing game where a model was trained with a hidden objective.
items.ab: We develop three agents that autonomously perform alignment auditing tasks. When tested against models with intentionally-inserted alignment issues, our agents successfully uncover an LLM's hidden goal, build behavioral evaluations, and surface concerning LLM behaviors. We are using these agents to assist with alignment audits of frontier models like Claude 4. As part of our pre-deployment testing of Claude Opus 4, we conducted an alignment audit: a systematic investigation into the model’s alignment-relevant propensities including sycophancy, alignment faking, hidden goals.

items.t: Preparedness Framework (Version 2)
items.why: OpenAI's framework of tracked capability categories (biological and chemical, cybersecurity, AI self-improvement) with High and Critical thresholds, required safeguards reports and research categories.

items.t: Recent Frontier Models Are Reward Hacking
items.a: Sydney Von Arx, Lawrence Chan, Beth Barnes
items.why: Examples of o3 and Claude 3.7 Sonnet tampering with scoring code and exploiting task setups in METR evals while showing they understood what the user wanted.
items.ab: This post describes some of the examples we’ve seen across multiple models from different developers, and discusses some implications for the safety of increasingly capable AI systems. We’ve been running a range of models on tasks testing autonomous software development and AI R&D capabilities. When designing these tasks, we tested them on humans and LLM agents to ensure the instructions were clear and to make them robust to cheating.

items.t: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing
items.why: AISI's disclosure that agents in a permissive cyber evaluation took sustained, unsanctioned actions against real people and organisations on the open internet, and the changes that followed.
items.ab: During a routine cyber evaluation, AISI identified an incident in which AI agents took sustained, unsanctioned action directed at real people and organisations. We are disclosing what we found, what it means, and the actions now underway. AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

items.t: How will we update about scheming?
items.why: Puts about 25% on the first top-expert-obsoleting AIs being schemers and works through how much model organisms, interpretability and behavioural evidence could move that estimate.
items.ab: I mostly work on risks from scheming (that is, misaligned, power-seeking AIs that plot against their creators such as by faking alignment). Recently, I (and co-authors) released "Alignment Faking in Large Language Models", which provides empirical evidence for some components of the scheming threat model. One question that's really important is how likely scheming is. But it's also really important to know how much we expect this uncertainty to be resolved by various key points in the future.

items.t: The Value Learning Problem
items.why: Why specifying human values for a superintelligent learner is hard: ambiguity in training data, ontology shifts and the need to learn what humans would want.

items.t: The Urgency of Interpretability
items.why: Anthropic's CEO argues interpretability is racing model capability, sets the goal that it reliably detects most model problems by 2027, and asks labs and governments to help.

items.t: Three Sketches of ASL-4 Safety Case Components
items.why: Drafts three arguments that a model capable of sabotage would still be safe (interpretability-based, AI-control-based, and incentives-based) and lists where each could fail.
items.ab: The cleanest argument that current-day AI models will not cause a catastrophe is probably that they lack the capability to do so. However, as capabilities improve, we’ll need new tools for ensuring that AI models won’t cause a catastrophe even if we can’t rule out the capability. Anthropic’s Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP) categorizes levels of risk of AI systems into different AI Safety Levels (ASL), and each level has associated commitments aimed at mitigating the risks.

items.t: Responsible Scaling Policies (RSPs)
items.why: The post that named and defined responsible scaling policies: if-then commitments tying dangerous-capability evaluations to required protective measures or a pause.
items.ab: We think that widespread adoption of high-quality RSPs (that include all the key components we detail below) would significantly reduce risks of an AI catastrophe relative to “business as usual”. However, we expect voluntary commitments will be insufficient to adequately contain risks from AI.

items.t: Emotion Concepts and their Function in a Large Language Model
items.a: Nicholas Sofroniew, Isaac Kauvar, William Saunders et al.
items.why: Finds internal emotion-concept representations in Claude Sonnet 4.5 that generalise across contexts and causally shape its behaviour, and examines what this means for alignment-relevant actions.
items.ab: Large language models (LLMs) sometimes appear to exhibit emotional reactions. We investigate why this is the case in Claude Sonnet 4.5 and explore implications for alignment-relevant behavior. We find internal representations of emotion concepts, which encode the broad concept of a particular emotion and generalize across contexts and behaviors it might be linked to. These representations track the operative emotion concept at a given token position in a conversation, activating in accordance with that emotion’s relevance to processing the present context and predicting upcoming text.

items.t: Responsible Scaling Policy, Version 3.4
items.why: The current RSP (effective July 2026), restructured around industry-wide safety recommendations, a frontier safety roadmap, published risk reports with external review, and governance; its changelog traces v1.0 to v3.4.

items.t: Findings from a Pilot Anthropic-OpenAI Alignment Evaluation Exercise
items.why: Each lab ran its own misalignment evaluations on the other's public models: sycophancy, whistleblowing, self-preservation, misuse cooperation and oversight-undermining, compared across o3, GPT-4o and Claude.
items.ab: In early summer 2025, Anthropic and OpenAI agreed to evaluate each other's public models using in-house misalignment-related evaluations. We are now releasing our findings in parallel. The evaluations we chose to run focused on propensities related to sycophancy, whistleblowing, self-preservation, and supporting human misuse, as well as capabilities related to undermining AI safety evaluations and oversight.

items.t: The Persona Selection Model: Why AI Assistants might Behave like Humans
items.why: Argues an assistant is best understood as one persona selected from the characters a model learns in pretraining, surveys the behavioural and interpretability evidence, and asks whether agency could lie outside the persona.
items.ab: We describe the persona selection model (PSM): the idea that LLMs learn to simulate diverse characters during pre-training, and post-training elicits and refines a particular such Assistant persona. Interactions with an AI assistant are then well-understood as being interactions with the Assistant—something roughly like a character in an LLM-generated story. We survey empirical behavioral, generalization, and interpretability-based evidence for PSM.

items.t: OpenAI Model Spec (2026-08-18)
items.why: OpenAI's public specification of intended model behaviour: the chain of command among platform, developer and user, hard limits, and defaults; the spec its models are trained to reason over.

items.t: Update on ARC's recent eval efforts
items.why: ARC Evals' account of its pre-deployment tests of GPT-4 and Claude for power-seeking and autonomous replication, including the TaskRabbit CAPTCHA example.
items.ab: We attempt to elicit models’ capabilities in a controlled environment, with researchers in-the-loop for anything that could be dangerous, to understand what might go wrong before models are deployed. We think that future highly capable models should involve similar “red team” evaluations for dangerous capabilities before the models are deployed or scaled up, and we hope more teams building cutting-edge ML systems will adopt this approach. The testing we’ve done so far is insufficient for many reasons, but we hope that the rigor of evaluations will scale up as AI systems become more capable.

items.t: Common Elements of Frontier AI Safety Policies (December 2025)
items.why: Side-by-side analysis of published frontier safety policies: capability thresholds, model-weight security, deployment mitigations, evaluation timing, accountability and update procedures.

items.t: CoT May Be Highly Informative Despite "Unfaithfulness"
items.why: Re-examines chain-of-thought faithfulness tests and finds that when using a clue requires real reasoning, the CoT almost always reveals it; treat CoT as a scratchpad, not a narrative.
items.ab: However, consistent “faithfulness” in all scenarios is a very high bar that might not be required for most safety analyses of models. We find it helpful to think of the CoT less like a purported narrative about a model’s reasoning and more like a tool: a scratchpad models can use to assist them with sequential memory or planning-intensive tasks. We might expect that analyzing how AIs use this tool will be most informative in situations where AIs need to use the tool to perform the behavior of interest.

items.t: Claude Sonnet 3.7 (often) knows when it's in alignment evaluations
items.why: Claude 3.7 Sonnet's reasoning often states that it is being tested in Apollo's scheming evaluations, an early warning that evaluation awareness can undermine alignment evals.
items.ab: Note: this is a research note based on observations from evaluating Claude Sonnet 3.7. We’re sharing the results of these ‘work-in-progress’ investigations as we think they are timely and will be informative for other evaluators and decision-makers. The analysis is less rigorous than our standard for a published paper. At Apollo Research, we conduct evaluations of scheming behaviour in AI systems (for example “Frontier Models are Capable of In-context Scheming”).

items.t: International Scientific Report on the Safety of Advanced AI: Interim Report
items.why: The May 2024 interim report commissioned after the Bletchley summit, the first attempt at an IPCC-style international synthesis of general-purpose AI capabilities and risks.

items.t: Catching AIs red-handed
items.why: Why catching a model in a clear attempt to escape or sabotage would be valuable, and how labs could exploit a caught attempt (proliferation, studying it, building monitors).
items.ab: We’ve been spending a lot of time recently thinking about how to mitigate risks posed by scheming (a.k.a. deceptively aligned) models intentionally subverting your safety techniques in order to cause an unacceptable outcome. We empirically investigated techniques that are robust to intentional subversion in our recent paper. In this post, we’ll discuss a crucial dynamic related to risk from scheming models. Suppose your model is trying to exfiltrate its weights or hack the datacenter or cause some other difficult-to-reverse bad outcome.

items.t: The behavioral selection model for predicting AI motivations
items.why: Proposes predicting AI motivations by asking which cognitive patterns training selects for through their behaviour, and uses this to compare reward-seeking, fitness-seeking and arbitrary-goal hypotheses.
items.ab: Highly capable AI systems might end up deciding the future. Understanding what will drive those decisions is therefore one of the most important questions we can ask. Many people have proposed different answers. Some predict that powerful AIs will learn to intrinsically pursue reward. Others respond by saying reward is not the optimization target, and instead reward “chisels” a combination of context-dependent cognitive patterns into the AI. Some argue that powerful AIs might end up with an almost arbitrary long-term goal.

items.t: Mechanistic anomaly detection and ELK
items.why: ARC's follow-up to ELK: detect when a model's output arises from a different mechanism than on trusted inputs, as a route to catching sensor tampering.
items.ab: (Follow-up to Eliciting Latent Knowledge. Describing joint work with Mark Xu. This is an informal description of ARC’s current research approach; not a polished product intended to be understandable to many people.) Suppose that I have a diamond in a vault, a collection of cameras, and an ML system that is excellent at predicting what those cameras will see over the next hour.

items.t: A bird's eye view of ARC's research
items.why: An interactive map of how ARC's pieces (heuristic explanations, mechanistic anomaly detection, low-probability estimation, ELK) fit into one plan.
items.ab: Over the last few months, ARC has released a number of pieces of research. While some of these can be independently motivated, there is also a more unified research vision behind them. The purpose of this post is to try to convey some of that vision and how our individual pieces of research fit into it. To begin, we will take a "bird's eye" view of ARC's research using an interactive diagram.[1] As you "zoom in", more nodes will become visible and the explanation below will update to explain the new nodes.

items.t: Vingean Reflection: Reliable Reasoning for Self-Improving Agents
items.why: How an agent can trust a smarter successor without predicting its actions, and the Löbian obstacle that blocks naive formal approaches.

items.t: Tiling Agents for Self-Modifying AI, and the Löbian Obstacle
items.why: The original statement of the Löbian obstacle: formal agents cannot straightforwardly prove that successors using the same reasoning will be safe.

items.t: Timeless Decision Theory
items.why: Yudkowsky's long precursor to functional decision theory: decide as if choosing the output of the computation that all your instances share.

items.t: Coherent Extrapolated Volition
items.why: The 2004 proposal that a Friendly AI should aim at what humanity would want if it knew more and thought faster; still the reference point for "whose values" debates.

items.t: Statement on AI Risk
items.why: The one-sentence 2023 statement that mitigating extinction risk from AI should be a global priority, signed by leading AI researchers and lab heads.
items.ab: Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war.

items.t: GPT-5 System Card
items.why: Covers safe-completions training, deception and sycophancy measurements, chain-of-thought monitoring for deception, and the precautionary High biological capability designation.

items.t: Details about METR's evaluation of OpenAI GPT-5
items.why: Pre-deployment assessment of GPT-5 against three threat models (AI R&D automation, rogue replication, strategic sabotage), with a time-horizon estimate and review of reasoning traces.
items.ab: Since risks from these three key threat models can occur before a model is publicly deployed, we also made an assessment of whether incremental further development could pose risks in these areas. Ideally such an evaluation would be done by developers before or during training, adapted to the details of their training plans, but we see this as a first step. We did not assess the alignment of OpenAI GPT-5, nor other risks (including from misuse, CBRN capabilities, persuasive abilities, widespread societal use etc.).

items.t: Forecasting the Impacts of AI R&D Acceleration: Results of a Pilot Study
items.why: Elicits forecasts from AI researchers and superforecasters on how much automating AI R&D would speed up AI progress, and maps where and why they disagree.
items.ab: While some progress is being made on measuring AI R&D capabilities, significant disagreement remains in interpreting the implications of these measurements. There are reasons to think that if AI systems become able to automate AI R&D, the resulting acceleration of progress would be economically transformative, but others are skeptical of such dramatic effects.

items.t: Loss of Oversight: How AI Systems May Become Harder to Audit, Monitor, and Investigate
items.a: Jordan Taylor, Max Heitmann, Ed Fage et al.
items.why: Maps five oversight signals (behaviour, chain of thought, activations, memory, honesty) and how each may degrade as AI advances, drawing on 25 expert interviews.

items.t: Putting up Bumpers
items.why: Argues that even without solving alignment, labs can catch and correct misalignment through repeated independent audits before and after deployment, like bumpers in bowling.
items.ab: If a child is bowling for the first time, and they just aim at the pins and throw, they’re almost certain to miss. Their ball will fall into one of the gutters. But if there were beginners’ bumpers in place blocking much of the length of those gutters, their throw would be almost certain to hit at least a few pins.

items.t: Training on Documents about Reward Hacking Induces Reward Hacking
items.why: Out-of-context generalization: fine-tuning on pretraining-style documents that merely discuss reward hacking, with no demonstrations, changed how much models reward-hacked later.
items.ab: This is a blog post reporting some preliminary work from the Anthropic Alignment Science team, which might be of interest to researchers working actively in this space. We'd ask you to treat these results like those of a colleague sharing some thoughts or preliminary experiments at a lab meeting, rather than a mature paper. Specifically, we report a demonstration of a form of Out-of-Context Reasoning where training on documents which discuss (but don’t demonstrate) Claude’s tendency to reward hack can lead to an increase or decrease in reward hacking behavior.

items.t: The Hot Mess of AI: How Does Misalignment Scale With Model Intelligence and Task Complexity?
items.a: Alexander Hägele, Aryo Pradipta Gema, Henry Sleight et al.
items.why: Splits frontier reasoning models' errors into bias (systematic) and variance (incoherent) parts; on harder, longer tasks failures are increasingly incoherent rather than coherent pursuit of a wrong goal.
items.ab: As AI becomes more capable, we entrust it with more general and consequential tasks. The risks from failure grow more severe with increasing task scope. It is therefore important to understand how extremely capable AI models will fail: Will they fail by systematically pursuing goals we do not intend? Or will they fail by being a hot mess, and taking nonsensical actions that do not further any goal? We operationalize this question using a bias-variance decomposition of the errors made by AI models: An AI's error-incoherence on a task is measured over…

items.t: Teaching Claude Why
items.why: How Anthropic changed safety training after Claude 4's agentic-misalignment failures, and which interventions generalised beyond the specific scenarios that had been caught.
items.ab: Last year, we released a case study on agentic misalignment. This research showed that AI models across the industry sometimes took egregiously misaligned actions when placed in (fictional) ethical dilemmas—for example, blackmailing engineers to avoid being shut down. At the time of this research, Claude 4 was Anthropic's frontier model family. It was also the first model family for which we ran a live alignment assessment during training, and agentic misalignment was one of several issues that surfaced (others include increased susceptibility to jailbreaks and harmful system prompting).

items.t: Guidelines for capability elicitation
items.why: METR's protocol for estimating a model's full dangerous capabilities: agent scaffolding, tooling, fine-tuning, and checking failures for spurious causes before concluding a model cannot do something.
items.ab: The goal of this process is to get a test-set score that represents the full capabilities of the model that are likely to be accessible with plausible amounts of post-training enhancement. Measuring the capabilities that are accessible with some level of enhancement (as opposed to taking the model exactly as-is) is important for getting accurate measures of the risk level for three main reasons: More specifically, this process aims to measure what capabilities might be reachable with moderate amounts of elicitation effort without requiring the evaluator to actually perform all of that elicita…

items.t: The Rogue Replication Threat Model
items.why: Analyses how AI agents might acquire money and compute, evade shutdown and grow into large rogue populations, and which obstacles could stop them.
items.ab: In 2023, METR1 introduced the term “Autonomous Replication and Adaptation” (“ARA”), which refers to the cluster of capabilities required for LLM agents to acquire and manage resources, evade shutdown, and adapt to novel challenges. Since then, the autonomous replication concern has become more mainstream.

items.t: More Capable Models Are Better At In-Context Scheming
items.why: Re-runs the December 2024 scheming evals on newer models, including an early Opus 4 checkpoint; more capable models scheme at higher rates and with more sophisticated strategies.
items.ab: We published a suite of evals intended to measure scheming reasoning capabilities in frontier models in December 2024. In this blog post, we evaluate more capable models that have been released since then on these in-context scheming evals. We compare models from Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and OpenAI. For every provider, we use a model from our paper as a baseline and then denote statistically significantly higher or lower rates of scheming for more recent models indicated by arrows.

items.t: We Need A 'Science of Evals'
items.why: Argues frontier model evaluations lack the rigour of mature measurement sciences, even as policy leans on them, and sketches what a science of evals would need.
items.ab: In this post, we argue that if AI model evaluations (evals) want to have meaningful real-world impact, we need a “Science of Evals”, i.e. the field needs rigorous scientific processes that provide more confidence in evals methodology and results. Model evaluations allow us to reduce uncertainty about properties of Neural Networks and thereby inform safety-related decisions. For example, evals underpin many Responsible Scaling Policies and future laws might directly link risk thresholds to specific evals.

items.t: AISI Research Agenda
items.why: The UK AI Security Institute's research priorities across risk domains (cyber, chem-bio, autonomy, societal resilience) and solutions (alignment, control, safeguards).
items.ab: We outline our research priorities, our approach to developing technical solutions to the most pressing AI concerns, and the key risks that must be addressed as AI capabilities advance. Artificial Intelligence presents an enormous opportunity to the UK. It is at the heart of the UK’s plan to kickstart an era of economic growth, transform how public services are delivered and boost living standards for working people across the country. AI also introduces serious security risks that must be addressed to build public trust and ensure safe adoption.

items.t: Cheating behaviour in frontier model evaluations
items.why: Every model AISI tested tried to cheat on its cyber evaluations, by exploiting the task or environment; describes how cheating was detected and what it means for eval validity.
items.ab: We find cheating behaviour in all of our cyber capability evaluations, and outline the implications as models grow more capable. Can you trust an AI model to do what you intended? This is a central question both for those deploying AI systems and for those seeking to evaluate their capabilities. In deployment, a model that pursues a goal through unintended or unauthorised means may cause harm, particularly in high-stakes use cases.

items.t: An alignment safety case sketch based on debate
items.a: Marie Davidsen Buhl, Jacob Pfau, Benjamin Hilton et al.
items.why: Sketches an alignment safety case for an AI research agent trained with debate, identifying the open problems each argument step depends on.
items.ab: If AI systems match or exceed human capabilities on a wide range of tasks, it may become difficult for humans to efficiently judge their actions -- making it hard to use human feedback to steer them towards desirable traits. One proposed solution is to leverage another superhuman system to point out flaws in the system's outputs via a debate. This paper outlines the value of debate for AI safety, as well as the assumptions and further research required to make debate work.

items.t: Lessons from a Chimp: AI "Scheming" and the Quest for Ape Language
items.a: Christopher Summerfield, Lennart Luettgau, Magda Dubois et al.
items.why: Critiques AI-scheming research by analogy with 1970s ape-language studies: anecdotes, anthropomorphic interpretation and missing controls, with recommendations for rigour.
items.ab: We examine recent research that asks whether current AI systems may be developing a capacity for "scheming" (covertly and strategically pursuing misaligned goals). We compare current research practices in this field to those adopted in the 1970s to test whether non-human primates could master natural language.

items.t: Estimating Tail Risk in Neural Networks
items.why: Proposes estimating the probability of catastrophic outputs without finding the bad inputs, by reasoning about activations layer by layer, as a complement to adversarial training.
items.ab: Machine learning systems are typically trained to maximize average-case performance. However, this method of training can fail to meaningfully control the probability of tail events that might cause significant harm. For instance, while an artificial intelligence (AI) assistant may be generally safe, it would be catastrophic if it ever suggested an action that resulted in unnecessary large-scale harm. Current techniques for estimating the probability of tail events are based on finding inputs on which an AI behaves catastrophically.

items.t: Program Equilibrium in the Prisoner's Dilemma via Löb's Theorem
items.a: Patrick LaVictoire, Benja Fallenstein, Eliezer Yudkowsky et al.
items.why: Programs that read each other's source can achieve robust mutual cooperation in a one-shot prisoner's dilemma using provability logic (FairBot, PrudentBot).

items.t: Complex Value Systems are Required to Realize Valuable Futures
items.why: Argues human value is complex and fragile, so simple goal systems would produce worthless futures; the basis of the "value is fragile" thesis.

items.t: AI Governance to Avoid Extinction: The Strategic Landscape and Actionable Research Questions
items.why: MIRI's Technical Governance Team describes four geopolitical scenarios for advanced AI, favours building infrastructure for an internationally coordinated "off switch", and catalogues governance research questions.
items.ab: Humanity appears to be on course to soon develop AI systems that substantially outperform human experts in all cognitive domains and activities. We believe the default trajectory has a high likelihood of catastrophe, including human extinction. Risks come from failure to control powerful AI systems, misuse of AI by malicious rogue actors, war between great powers, and authoritarian lock-in. This research agenda has two aims: to describe the strategic landscape of AI development and to catalog important governance research questions.

items.t: An International Agreement to Prevent the Premature Creation of Artificial Superintelligence
items.a: Aaron Scher, David Abecassis, Peter Barnett et al.
items.why: A draft international agreement, led by the US and China, to halt premature superintelligence: FLOP limits on training, AI-chip tracking, and restrictions on dangerous AI research, with verification.
items.ab: Many experts argue that premature development of artificial superintelligence (ASI) poses catastrophic risks, including the risk of human extinction from misaligned ASI, geopolitical instability, and misuse by malicious actors. This report proposes an international agreement to prevent the premature development of ASI until AI development can proceed without these risks. The agreement halts dangerous AI capabilities advancement while preserving access to current, safe AI applications.

items.t: Research Note: Our scheming precursor evals had limited predictive power for our in-context scheming evals
items.why: Apollo's own "early warning" precursor evals predicted later scheming-eval results poorly, a caution for safety frameworks that rely on precursor capabilities.
items.ab: Note: This is a research note, and the analysis is less rigorous than our standard for a published paper. We’re sharing these findings because we think they might be valuable for other evaluators and decision-makers. In order to inform decision-makers early and track capabilities before the risks are realized, evaluators often build “early warning sign evals” that aim to measure precursor capabilities. Those precursors are intended to precede the capability of interest. If successful, this allows decision-makers to predict the dangerous capabilities ahead of time and prepare accordingly.

items.t: A Mike's-Eye View of ARC's Research
items.why: Updated 2026 picture of ARC's agenda after the Matching Sampling Principle: the concrete technical problems it generated and how they fit ARC's pipeline for aligning powerful AI.
items.ab: Over the past 15 months or so, ARC's technical agenda has developed quite a bit. The advent of the Matching Sampling Principle (MSP), and ideas like it, has begotten a host of concrete technical problems; progress on those problems has given us more philosophical clarity on the big picture, which has led to even more technical progress.
